A devout and pious man like yourself, t'was not entire wantonness, your desire to hear something other than religious, and since the Pastor has so eloquently withdrawn, I will give you a toast. For, you see, my dear Pastor, something of the old pagan, a spark of heathenism, is still glowing somewhere within us all. It has outlived century after century, from the time of the old Teutons. Once every year that spark is fanned into flame--it flames up high, and then it is called "The Fires of St. John." Once every year we have "free night." Then the witches ride upon their brooms--the same brooms with which their witchcraft was once driven out of them--with scornful laughter the wild hordes sweep across the tree-tops, up, up, high upon the Blocksberg! Then it is, when in our hearts awake those wild desires which our fates could not fulfill--and, understand me well, dared not fulfill--then, no matter what may be the name of the law that governs the world on that day, in order that that one single wish may become a reality, by whose grace we prolong our miserable existence, thousand others must miserably perish. Part because they were never attainable; but the others, yes, the others, because we allowed them to escape us like wild birds, which, though already in our hands, but too listless to profit by opportunity, we failed to grasp at the right moment. But no matter. Once every year we have "free night." And yonder tongues of fire shooting up towards the heavens--do you know what they are? They are the spirits of our dead and perished wishes! That is the red plumage of our birds of paradise we might have petted and nursed through our entire lives, but have escaped us! That is the old chaos, the heathenism within us; and though we be happy in sunshine and according to law, to-night is St. John's night. To its ancient pagan fires I empty this glass. To-night they shall burn and flame up high--high--and again high! Will no one drink to my toast?
[Pause.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Trembling.] I will!
[They look into each other's eyes and clink glasses.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Hesitatingly.] I, too, George!

div.head: George.
div.p: [Stroking her hair sadly, patronizing.] Yes, yes; you, too.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Suddenly bursting out.] You--you idiots! What do you know about it, anyway? I--I didn't understand it myself, but I have a presentiment there is something sinful about it all!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: My dear Mr. von Harten, above all your heathenism watches our good old God, our Father, and therefore I fearlessly drink to your toast.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Well, well, I'll not be the only exception. [Drinks also. A glow much nearer, behind the trees. Louder yelling and laughter.] Well, what is it now?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: They are dangerously near the sheds now.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Didn't I tell you to take the proper precautions?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: I did. They had only three tar-barrels early this evening. Where they got the fourth from, I don't know.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: I'll wager they found the barrel of axle-grease! Why didn't you lock it up?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: You know yourself, on this day no lock or key is of any avail.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Don't talk nonsense, but see what's to be done. I will be there myself, presently. Be quick! [Paul exits.] I can't depend on anybody these days! Where is my hat? [Marie gets it.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Can't we go, too, papa?

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Will you come, wife?

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: Yes, gladly, but stop scolding. There isn't a breath of air stirring, and therefore no danger.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Come along, Pastor!
[Exit Brauer, George, Gertrude and Mrs. Brauer .]

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Won't you accompany us, Miss Marie?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, thank you, Pastor!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Then may I remain with you for a while?

div.head: Several Voices.
div.p: [Outside, calling.] Pastor, Pastor!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: [Speaks through door.] I will be with you in a moment! [To Marie.] Well, may I!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Why, certainly, if it gives you pleasure!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Pleasure is hardly the proper word. I wanted to thank you for insisting upon my writing the bridal-poem. It has been a work of pleasure, I assure you. Do you like it?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: It is very nice. Pastor!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Have you memorized it already?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I think so!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Then would you mind reciting it for me? Come, I will assist you: "The flowers, the beautiful blossoms"---- Well?---- "are a maiden's----"

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, Pastor!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: You are acting so strangely to-day! You are so shy--so----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: The St. John's night oppresses me!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: That will soon be over.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Would that it were over now!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Perhaps the thought of traveling alone at night has something to do with it?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Oh! [Recovering herself--lightly.] You are right, Pastor; but it can't be helped!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Shall I come with you? Oh, I'll find something to be done in the city. I won't even have to ask permission. Anyway, I am longing for a glimpse of the good old town. I will inform the old pastor--I don't think he has retired as yet----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Then please tell him---- I usually visit him myself every day, but now, just before the wedding, it's impossible for me to call. Will you please tell him that? I am so fond of him! Tell him that, and in thought I kiss his hand.

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Certainly. And may I accompany you!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, thank you. Pastor!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Now let us speak openly, Miss Marie. I have been watching you all the evening. You appear to me--what shall I call it--like a mouse before a cat! You need a protector; some one in whom you can confide, some one----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: And so you would like to be my father confessor! Eh, Pastor?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: You know very well we do not have that institution in the Protestant Church, though at times it might prove a blessing----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Mischievously.] And then again it might not?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: You are quite right. We should all rely more upon ourselves----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [With emphasis.] I do that, Pastor, I do!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Yes, my dear Marie--pardon me, I should not have said that--and yet I must speak frankly with you; you seem to have a fear--a dread----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Of the cat?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I wish I knew!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: But supposing I were the cat, who would then be the mouse?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: That would be sinful and wicked in you!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: But one cannot be the cat and the mouse at the same time?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Yes, one can! But he who does, plays with his own destruction!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: And if one destroys one's self, who cares?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: You should not talk like that, Miss Marie.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Oh, it is all nonsense, all nonsense, for to-night is St. John's night. Do you see that fire yonder. Pastor? They had to put it out! But there, on the hill--look, there, there! How beautiful! How wild!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Yes, and when you look closely, it is nothing more than a mass of dirty lumber.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: For shame, Pastor!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Like everything that blazes, except the sun----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: You should not have said that, Pastor--you should not. I don't want it! I will not have you slander my St. John's fires! I want to enjoy it once--only once--then nevermore!!!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: [Disturbed.] My dear Miss Marie, I do not understand the reason for your agitation, and I will not question you! But of your struggles--you shall know that you have a friend near you, on whom you can rely, now and for all time to come. Marie, I don't know how to express myself; but I desire to shield and protect you all your life--I will worship you----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Pastor, do you know who and what I am?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I do!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: And who my mother is?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I know all!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Pastor, how am I to understand this?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Marie, I know I should not have spoken, at least not now. I should have waited--it was stupid of me, I know; but I have such a fear--a fear for you. You are going to the city to-night and I don't know what may happen! But you shall know before you go, where you belong and that your future is assured!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [With a sigh of relief--almost a sob.] Ah--ah--ah----!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Marie, I do not want an answer now. Besides, I must first notify my father. Though he is but a simple farmer, he shall not be slighted-- Marie----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Shrinking--dully.] Yes, that is--perhaps--what I need--ah! [Sinks in chair.]

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Why, what is the matter? Shall I get you a glass of water? Or would you prefer wine?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [With an effort.] Wine--wine--there--in the bowl! [He helps her--she drinks.] Thank you! [Stirred.] No one has ever waited on me before!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I will carry you upon my hands

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Very well, Pastor; but no one must know before the wedding!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Perhaps on the wedding day--at the wedding feast? Papa might make the announcement; that would be such a fitting occasion!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, no! I will have to much to do then.

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Then, when the happy pair have gone?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [With sudden, impulsive decision.] Yes, when they have gone!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: [Takes her hand.] Thank you. Miss Marie.
[Voices are heard outside.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Sh--[Withdrawing her hand.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Enters.] Ah, here you are, Pastor; we have been looking for you everywhere!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I am coming now, Miss Gertrude.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: It's too late, Pastor, they are all returning!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Impossible! Well, well, how the time passes, and one hardly knows how!
[Exit Pastor.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Embracing Gertrude.] Will you forgive me, darling?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Timidly.] I have nothing to forgive!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Do not say that! I have done everything--everything--you must----
[Enter all.]

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Well, my dear Pastor, time stands still for no one; so you had better stop excusing yourself and empty your glass. 'Twill all come out right in the end.

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I think I had better go now; for here every one is making fun of me.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Pastor, I need hardly tell you, that you are always welcome in this house.

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I am sure of it, Mr. Brauer! If I did not think so, I would not take that matter so lightly----

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Jokingly threatens him with finger.] Pastor----

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: [With a happy glance at Marie.] Good-night. [Shakes hands with all.]

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Good-night!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Good-night, Miss Marie!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Shaking his hand.] Good-night, Pastor! [George, with a questioning glance, advances a step or two.]

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: George, see the Pastor to the gate!

div.head: George.
div.p: [As though awakening.] Yes, uncle.
[Both exit.]

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: Well, Henry, everything has quieted down!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: It's about time, too! Why, its eleven o'clock! Come, let's to bed.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Good-night, papa!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Affectionately.] Good-night, my pet!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Good-night!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: By the bye--when will you be back?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: To-morrow, about ten, papa!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Now be careful; no unnecessary exertions--understand? The day of the wedding will be hard enough on all of us.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, papa dear! [Kisses him.]

div.head: George.
div.p: [Enters at this moment.] We have still an hour and a quarter till train time. I will wait for you here, Marie.

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: You might help each other pass away the time.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: I want to sit up, too.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Tut, tut, ray pet; you go to bed, you need the rest.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Whiningly.] Well then, good-night.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [In silent fear.] I can't stay here---- Mama, I want to ask you about something----

div.head: George.
div.p: Then you will come down in time for the train?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, in time for the train.

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: Good-night, George.

div.head: George.
div.p: Good-night, auntie!
[Exit Mrs. Brauer , Gertrude and Marie.]

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: You know where my cigars are?

div.head: George.
div.p: Yes!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: And if you need anything to keep you awake--I have left the key----

div.head: George.
div.p: [In monosyllables.] Thank you!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Well, what in----

div.head: George.
div.p: What's the matter---- Oh, my dear uncle, if I have failed to pay you the necessary respect, I beg your pardon.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Respect? Oh, damn you and your respect!

div.head: George.
div.p: Uncle----

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: See here, perhaps I did wrong?

div.head: George.
div.p: You--wrong? How?

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Have you forgotten what passed between us yesterday?

div.head: George.
div.p: My dear uncle, that seems to me so far, far away!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: It strikes me you are going at a pretty fast gait!

div.head: George.
div.p: At any rate, uncle, do not worry about it. It will all come out right in the end. [As he is listening towards the door, gives a sudden start.]

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: What's the matter?

div.head: George.
div.p: I thought I heard some one----

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Some one of the family perhaps, upstairs. Very well, then all is well, my boy! Good-night, my son.

div.head: George.
div.p: Good-night, uncle!
[Brauer exits, shaking his head.]

div.head: George.
div.p: [Sits at table--tries to read--listens, goes to door C.--calls out softly into the garden.] Who is there? [Still softer.] Is that you, Marie?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Whining outside.] It's only me!

div.head: George.
div.p: [Surprised.] Gertrude, what do you want?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Gertrude enters in nightgown and flowing hair.] I am so uneasy, George dear; I just wanted to look at you once more before going to sleep.

div.head: George.
div.p: But, little one, if papa should see you like this---- Quick, go back to your room.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: I cannot, my heart is so heavy.

div.head: George.
div.p: How so, dear?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: George, I have been thinking; I really am not good enough to be your wife.

div.head: George.
div.p: Wha--what nonsense----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: I am too silly--oh, yes; I never know what to say to you! I am so stupid.

div.head: George.
div.p: Why, my child--darling--pet----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: A while ago, out in the garden, and the moon shining so brightly, you walked by my side in deep silence----

div.head: George.
div.p: Why, mama was with us----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: George, it is yet time. If you love some one else----

div.head: George.
div.p: In heaven's name, child, have you ever mentioned this to any one?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Only to papa; he was very angry and scolded me dreadfully.

div.head: George.
div.p: H'm! Now listen to me, my pet----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Rather than make you unhappy, I would jump into the river----

div.head: George.
div.p: In the first place, your presence here in this condition is decidedly improper----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: But we are to be married in three days----

div.head: George.
div.p: So much more reason. [Stroking her hair.] What beautiful hair you have, dear!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Happily.] Do you like it?

div.head: George.
div.p: And in the second place, I will have none other than you. We will love each other very much. At first you will be my playmate--and then--later, perhaps--my real mate. Are you satisfied?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Yes, dear!

div.head: George.
div.p: And now, you must go to bed!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Then I will wrap myself in my hair--and I will dream of you and what you said--that it is beautiful--and so I will fall asleep. Good-night, George dear!

div.head: George.
div.p: [Kisses her on the forehead.] Good-night!
[He gloomily takes position at table with a sigh when Gertrudeexits, covering his face with his hands. Marie enters softly.]

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie, you have come----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: It is early yet, is it not?

div.head: George.
div.p: We have a full hour more. Have they all gone to bed?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I think so. All the lights are out.

div.head: George.
div.p: Come, sit here----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I--I--I think I will go back upstairs!

div.head: George.
div.p: No, no; here is something to read! You see, I'm reading myself.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Very well. [Sits.] But, George, I would really prefer to go to the depot alone.

div.head: George.
div.p: [Softly.] Marie! [She shuts her eyes.] Are you tired? [She shakes her head.] One whole hour I will have you all to myself!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: George----

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: The fires have all gone out, I suppose?

div.head: George.
div.p: Ah, yes; a small pyre of wood--it is soon burned down!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: And then it's as dark as ever!!! But, George, how beautifully you spoke this evening! I have never heard anything like it before.

div.head: George.
div.p: You were the only one who understood me.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No wonder! It was as though I spoke the words myself--that is, I don't mean to say----

div.head: George.
div.p: What, dear?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Oh, you know!

div.head: George.
div.p: But I don't know!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [After a pause.] George, I have something to confess to you. In fact, that is why I came down here so soon. You shall know it, you alone. I have this day given my hand----

div.head: George.
div.p: [With a start.] Marie!!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Astonished.] Well?

div.head: George.
div.p: To whom?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Why, to the pastor! Who else could it be? There is no one else!

div.head: George.
div.p: [Reproachfully.] Why did you do that? Why did you?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I have my whole life before me, and the fires [pointing to fields and to heart] will not burn forever----

div.head: George.
div.p: [Bitterly.] You should not have done it--you--it is a----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Sh--not so loud!

div.head: George.
div.p: But you do not love him at all!!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: How do you know?

div.head: George.
div.p: [Bitterly,] How? Of course, how should I? I don't know! Pardon me! Well, I congratulate you!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Quietly.] Thank you!

div.head: George.
div.p: But why am I the first one to be taken into your confidence? Why not uncle? We two have not been so intimate as----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, we two have not been very intimate--I only thought----

div.head: George.
div.p: So, then, we have both our burden; and we soon will have to part. Therefore we can now safely speak of the past. My manuscript you read! You even went so far as to perjure yourself on account of it. Oh, you don't mind a little thing like that! I wish I were the same! You know the subject of my verses, and we must now understand each other fully. Now, tell me openly, why, why did you treat me so unkindly, to say nothing worse, in former days?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Did I, George?

div.head: George.
div.p: 'Tis hardly necessary to remind you of all the indignities you heaped upon me. It almost seemed to me as if you purposely intended to drive me mad. Do you remember the day when I followed you into the cellar, and you turned and ran out and locked the door, and compelled me to remain there all night?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Smiling.] Yes, I remember!

div.head: George.
div.p: Why did you do that?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: That is very simple. You are Count von Harten--and I?--I am but a poor Lithuanian foundling--aye, worse than that. If you follow such a one into the cellar, she knows, or at least thinks she knows, your purpose.

div.head: George.
div.p: So, that was the reason! And at the same time you went under your manzanillo-tree to die?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Nods.]

div.head: George.
div.p: And did you never realize the real state of things? Gertrude was then still a child--and because I could not win you, I took her. Did that thought never occur to you?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: How could I ever dare to think that?

div.head: George.
div.p: But later?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: The day before yesterday, when I read your book, I felt it for the first time.

div.head: George.
div.p: And now, it is too late----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, now it is too late! Had I felt then as I do now, I would not have resisted you----

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie, do you know what you are saying?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Breaking out.] Oh I don't care, I don't care! It is my fate. You must rule and govern--and I--I must serve; and in the end--we both must die----

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie, you should be loved, you must be loved--beyond all senses--loved beyond all measure!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Pointing towards R.] He loves me!

div.head: George.
div.p: He?--Bah!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Don't be angry, George dear; you don't dare love me yourself. You can never be anything to me!

div.head: George.
div.p: No, never; for this house must be kept clean. No, no, this house must not be soiled. We would both suffocate in our shame. But we can think of what might have been; that is not sin, is it?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: What were your words? "They are the wild birds of paradise, that have escaped us." That was it, was it not? How beautiful!

div.head: George.
div.p: I don't remember!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: But I am not a wild bird, George; I am tame--so tame----

div.head: George.
div.p: You are tame?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: For you, George dear, only for you!!!

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie, my love! [Strokes her hair affectionally, then moves away.] No, no, we must be strong! Only a few minutes ago, Gertrude came softly down those stairs; if she should come again--my God----!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: What did she want?

div.head: George.
div.p: You can imagine----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: The poor thing! But you will love her?

div.head: George.
div.p: As well as possible! But then I must not think of you.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: But you must not think of me--and I will try and not think of you!

div.head: George.
div.p: Never, Marie?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Only occasionally--on holidays----

div.head: George.
div.p: Only then?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: And on St. John's eve----

div.head: George.
div.p: When the fires are burning?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, and when the fires are out, then I shall cry----

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie!!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, no, George, sit still--I will sit here. Some one might be in the garden, after all.

div.head: George.
div.p: They are all sound asleep!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Even so! We must be brave; not for mine--but for your sake, George.

div.head: George.
div.p: Why did you say that? What do you think of me?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I think you are hard-hearted.

div.head: George.
div.p: And yet you love me?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, I love you, for your own sake. For you have had to struggle and fight--and that is what made you what you are. I have also fought and struggled; but I have lost faith in myself--lost faith in everything. If you only knew!! Sometimes I am afraid of myself--sometimes I would commit murder, so restless and without peace I am.

div.head: George.
div.p: With me you would have found peace. We would have worked together and planned through half the nights--and you know how ambitious I am.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: And so am I, for you! You should be the first and greatest. They all shall bow before you--I myself will kneel before you and say to you: "You love to rule and command? Now rule--now command!!!!!!"
[Throws herself before him--her arms around his knees, looking up.]

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie, in heaven's name rise! If any one should see you so----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Let them see me----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Rising.] You are right. It was low in me. But he who originates where I do, is low--so low----

div.head: George.
div.p: Don't think of it, Marie! Think of this house and all the love it has given you!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: How quiet everything is--not a sound to be heard--as silent as the grave----

div.head: George.
div.p: Then be content, for they have buried us together!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: If they only had----!

div.head: George.
div.p: And see the pale moon--how it throws its silvery rays over the garden--and yonder is your manzanillo-tree.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, yes, do you see it?

div.head: George.
div.p: And its white, trembling leaves; see, see, each one seems alive--though not a breath of air is stirring. Come, let us go to it.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Cowering.] No, no, I think it is time--we must----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: What is it?

div.head: George.
div.p: There--something moved. It must be Gertrude. [Goes to door C. and calls.] "Gertrude!!!"
[Short pause.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: You must have been mistaken!

div.head: George.
div.p: No, no; I saw a shadow. "Gertrude!" Remain here, I'll go see! [Exit into garden.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Oh, I'm so afraid, George--so afraid----!
[Pause.]
[George returns, pale and agitated, trying to control himself.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Who was it? Who was it?

div.head: George.
div.p: Oh, no one--no one----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, there was--I can see it in your face!! Was it Gertrude?

div.head: George.
div.p: No.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Then it was papa?

div.head: George.
div.p: No, no.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: George, you are as pale as death; What has happened? Tell me!

div.head: George.
div.p: Nothing, nothing! There was a stranger in the garden--I sent him away.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: What stranger?

div.head: George.
div.p: [Pained.] Do not ask me!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Dully.] Oh, I know--I know! It was--my mother----

div.head: George.
div.p: Well, since you have said it----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: What did she want? But why do I ask? [Covers her face with her hands.] Oh, my God--my God!!!!

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Suddenly.] Close the blinds--I have a fear--tight--so!! Now put up the bars--so--and here, so--so----

div.head: George.
div.p: [Embracing her.] Marie! my darling!!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Hold me tight!!!

div.head: George.
div.p: Like this?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, like that! [She moves close to him.] Here I want to sit still----

div.head: George.
div.p: [Looks at watch.] If we only have time to catch that train---- [The whistle of a locomotive is heard in the distance. He starts.] Did you hear that?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Smilingly.] Yes!

div.head: George.
div.p: What was it?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: It was the train!

div.head: George.
div.p: Can you hear it this far?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: At night you can!

div.head: George.
div.p: [Sinks into chair L. of table, back to audience.]
My God! what shall we do now?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Softly.] I will tell you what we will do! We will sit still here--quietly--till the next train--till four o'clock!!!!
Throws herself upon George, passionately kissing him.]

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie! My love, my all! [Kisses her.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Kiss me again! Now, then, do you understand me? I am my own master, and care not for myself---- To-night is St. John's night!!!!!!!

div.head: George.
div.p: And the fires are burning low----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, no; let them burn----

div.head: George.
div.p: Yes, yes; let them burn--they shall burn!!!!!
[Marie disengages herself.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Kiss me no more--let me kiss you--I will take all upon myself--I will take all the consequences--my mother is a thief, and so am I! George--
[Throws herself into his arms with complete abandon.]
[Lights out. Curtain.]

div.head: ACT FOUR
div.p: Same setting. Morning. Centre table is decorated with flowers. Brauer, George and Gertrude are on veranda at rise of curtain. In open door, C., Mrs. Brauer. All listening to quartet, singing, "This is the day of our Lord" by Kreutzer. As curtain rises, Katie enters, L., listens also, and dries her eyes. At the end of the serenade, Brauer starts to make an address, and with George and Gertrude leaves the veranda.

div.head: Katie.
div.p: Mrs. Brauer, I would like to speak to you a moment.

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: [Wiping her eyes.] What is it, Katie?

div.head: Katie.
div.p: [Sniveling.] Oh, I'm so happy----
[Church bells are heard softly in the distance.]

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: There go the church bells. Have you put plenty of wine and luncheon in the arbor?

div.head: Katie.
div.p: Yes, ma'am! Miss Marie and I have prepared a lot!

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: What did you want to see me about?

div.head: Katie.
div.p: I wanted to ask you about the roast; shall we put it in the oven now, and just warm it up for dinner? Miss Marie thinks----

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: Never mind! I'll be down in the kitchen in a moment!

div.head: Katie.
div.p: And another thing, Mrs. Brauer; won't you please try and get Miss Marie to take a little rest? She has been hard at work since two o'clock this morning, and all day yesterday she was in the city. She can't stand it.

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: Oh, on a day like this, we must all put our shoulders to the wheel.

div.head: Katie.
div.p: Ah, Mrs. Brauer, you and I are old, and not much good for anything but work; but we must spare our young people. Why, at times she almost gives out.

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: Well, I will come and see for myself.

div.head: Katie.
div.p: Thank you!!! Oh, such a day!!! I am so happy---- [Exit both L.]

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Enters with George and Gertrude.] Thank goodness, that's over. Let me see: first it was the old soldiers, then the Turners, and now the Singing Society---- But do you know, I am so sick of all this wine--give me a brandy.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Gets drink from sideboard.] Yes, papa!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [To George.] And what's the matter with you?

div.head: George.
div.p: [With a sigh.] Nothing!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Imitating him.] Nothing!!! I can't quite make you out---- Here, have a drink?

div.head: George.
div.p: No, thank you!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Well, then, don't! Your health, my pet!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Drink hearty, papa!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Rises.] The carriage will arrive here sharply at ten! Understand?

div.head: George.
div.p: Yes!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: And your friend from the city--we will find him at the station?

div.head: George.
div.p: Yes; he arrives quarter to ten.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: For we must have two witnesses.--Do you know what I would like? [Tapping him on breast.] I would like to be able to look in there.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Oh, let him alone, papa! He is now my George. If I am satisfied with him----

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: You are right! He who gets my child can laugh--but he also shall laugh. Understand? [Exit R.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Never mind him, George dear. You need not laugh if you don't want to. Not on my account. [Bells.] Do you hear, George? The church bells, ringing softly, singing, like human voices!!!! That is for you and me!!

div.head: George.
div.p: Why for us?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: It is the old pastor's desire; half an hour this morning, and then again this afternoon, when we exchange rings. Do you know, George, mama says a bride's dream the night before her wedding is surely an omen. Do you believe that?

div.head: George.
div.p: [Preoccupied.] Yes.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: I dreamed last night of a large, yellow wheat-field, in which a poor little rabbit had hidden itself; and high above, in the air, I saw a large hawk. Then it appeared to me that I was the little rabbit, and in fear and dread I called out "George! George!" when suddenly it shot down upon me!--just think----

div.head: George.
div.p: And then?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Then I awoke. The cold perspiration stood thickly upon my brow---- Oh, George dear, you will protect me? You won't let any one hurt me, will you? For I am only a poor little rabbit, after all----

div.head: George.
div.p: [Staring before him.] My God!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: George, I wanted to ask you something.

div.head: George.
div.p: Well?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: You don't love some one else, do you?

div.head: George.
div.p: [Disturbed.] But, my child----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Well, you know that if a bride cannot laugh on her wedding day, she loves another----

div.head: George.
div.p: Why, nonsense----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Unshaken.] Oh, yes, George; I read it myself. And even if you do, George, I feel so--my love for you is so great, it could move mountains. I love you so dearly---- She will surely learn to forget you, I will love you so much.

div.head: George.
div.p: But, my pet----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: No, no, George. You see, I don't blame you so much. How could I? For what am I, compared to other women?--George, does she love you so very much?

div.head: George.
div.p: Who?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Oh, you know. But don't worry, George dear; she will forget you in time! Don't you remember Robert, our neighbor's son? He threatened to kill himself if I didn't marry him, and he has already forgotten me! And to-day, when we stand at the altar, at the Doxology and the exchange of rings, I will nudge you softly, and then we will both pray to our good Father in heaven to make it easy for her; for no one shall be unhappy on this day! Why, George, you are crying!!!!

div.head: George.
div.p: Crying--I?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Why, yes! Here are two large tears running down your cheek. [Wipes his eyes with her handkerchief.] So there----

div.head: George.
div.p: Tell me, my pet; and if we should be parted, after all?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: How could that be possible?

div.head: George.
div.p: If I should die--or----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Embracing him.] No, no! Don't say that! Don't say that!!!
[Marie appears in door, seeing embrace.]

div.head: George.
div.p: [Startled.] Some one is here----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: It is only Marie.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Pointedly.] You seem to be particularly affectionate to-day.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Miffed.] We always love each other. Oh, perhaps that doesn't please you----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: It is nothing to me!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Half Jesting.] Besides, what do you want here? Isn't there anything to do in the kitchen?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Stung, but controlling herself.] Mama has sent me----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Yes, yes, dear; you are just in time to dress my hair. Have you hairpins?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Shaking her head.] I will get some. [Reels.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Affectionately.] What's the matter, dear? Oh, you must be tired!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I am not tired.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Yes, yes, you are. Now you sit down here. I will fetch them myself. [Quick exit.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Full of fear.] Gertrude!!!

div.head: George.
div.p: I must speak with you!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Speak; I am listening.

div.head: George.
div.p: Why this tone? Does it perhaps mean that between us all is over?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: If it is or is not, it matters little.

div.head: George.
div.p: Am I, then, to understand----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: My God! Have you not Gertrude? But now I saw her in your arms! What do you want with me?

div.head: George.
div.p: I must speak with you----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Not now----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Re-enters.] Here are the hairpins. [Marie takes them.] I have also brought my dressing-sacque and combs. Now we will excuse you for a little while, George dear. You can give your judgment later.

div.head: George.
div.p: [With a glance at Marie.] May I not remain?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: No, no. You would criticise and find fault, and embarrass Marie, and me, too. Now be good, George, and go into the garden. [George exits.]

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Holding sacque.] Will you put this on?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: No, I will put it around me.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: As you please. How do you want your hair dressed, high or low?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: But Marie, we had decided upon that! Have you forgotten?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Oh, pardon me--I--of course we had!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Then give me a kiss!
[Marie suddenly takes her head in both hands and stares at her.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Frightened.] Why do you look at me so strangely?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Embraces her fiercely] My darling!!!!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Oh, you hurt me!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Perhaps you hurt me, too----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: I? How so?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Has begun to comb.] How can you ask? You are about to be married--and--and--I--I am jealous of you!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Just wait, Marie, dear. [Sings.]
"In a year, in a year, when the nightingale comes----"

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Intensely.] When the nightingale comes?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: You will be Pastor's wife. [Laughs.]
[Marie, with one braid in her hand, bending back, laughing loudly and forced.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [In pain.] Oh, you are pulling my hair----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Any one as happy as you should be able to bear a little pain. There! I will braid it into your hair--for you are happy, are you not? Very happy?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Yes! I am--that is--I would like to be--but George--he is so sad.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: George?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Yes!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Lurkingly.] Perhaps you were right! Perhaps he does love another!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Softly groaning.] Oh, why did you say that?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Because---- No, no--how could he? That was wicked in me, wasn't it? How could he think of another, when he looks at you?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: No, no, Marie, you are right! I told him so myself!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Slowly and marked.] And what did he say?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: He?--He said nothing! And then--he cried----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Triumphantly.] He cried? George cried? Have you ever seen him do that before?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: No, never!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [To herself.] He cried----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: And then he said: "What if we should be parted, after all?"

div.head: Marie.
div.p: If who should be parted--you and he?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Yes--if he should die----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: If he--oh, that is what he meant! Oh, well, he just wanted to say something. [With forced lightness.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Of course he did. But what about the other woman? Oh, I didn't let him see that I cared--and for the time I didn't care, really; but now, when I think of it! My God!--if it were really so! If I only knew!!!!!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Of course, he would not tell you!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Do you think he would tell any one else?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, sooner than tell you.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Yes! I suppose so!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Shall I ask him?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Oh, if you would do that for me----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: There now, it is done. Here is the comb and the rest of the hairpins. Now go!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: And do you really think he would tell you?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I am sure he will.

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Oh, Marie, how grateful I shall be to you----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Pushes her out of the door.] Go now, go! [Stretches herself.] Ah--ah--ah---- [Calls softly.] George! [There is a knock at the door.] Come in!

div.head: Paul.
div.p: [Enters.] Pardon me, Miss Marie; is Mr. Brauer in?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, Mr. Paul!

div.head: Paul.
div.p: The assistant pastor would like to speak to him--but here he is, himself.

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: [Enters.] Good-morning, Miss Marie!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Offers her hand hesitatingly.] Good-morning!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: I will wait here, Mr. Paul!

div.head: Paul.
div.p: Then, Miss Marie, will you please give me the key to the cellar? I want to put the beer on the ice.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Gets key from keyboard.] Here it is.

div.head: Paul.
div.p: Thank you!
[Exit.]
[Pause.]

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: And have you nothing to say to me?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: What shall I say, Pastor?

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Are you not happy this day?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Hard.] No!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Not even on account of our betrothal?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: We will have no betrothal, Pastor!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: What are you saying?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I shall leave this place----

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: You----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: To-day, I leave this house!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Pardon me, if I have forced my attentions upon you----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No! You have not!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: My attentions were honorable, I assure you----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Thank you, Pastor, I know that; but----

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Then it is not on my account you are leaving?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Certainly not!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Does any one here know of your intention?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No one!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Miss Marie, I am still a young man; if I should mention such a word as "life's happiness," it would, perhaps, sound absurd. Therefore, I will not speak of myself. My fate is in my own hands. But if you realize this moment what you owe to this house--and I say this not for mine, nor for their sake, I say it for yours and yours alone; though I am but a poor mortal--it pains me--but be that as it may--Marie, if you cause a discord in this house, the blame will rest upon yourself.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Perhaps!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Pardon me--I will not question you. I wish to know nothing; that, in the end, is always the best. Did I not love you as well as myself, I would not speak another word; but as matters stand now, I will say one--aye, one more word--I would not have dared to say otherwise. The greatest, the highest thing one possesses in this world, is his life's melody--a certain strain that ever vibrates, that his soul forever sings--waking or dreaming, loudly or softly, internally or externally. Others may say: "His temperament or his character is so, or so." He only smiles, for he knows his melody and he knows it alone. You see, Miss Marie, my life's happiness you have destroyed, but my life's melody you can not take from me. That is pure and will always remain so. And now I say to you, Miss Marie, if you fill this house, where you have obtained everything you possess--honor, bread, and love--if you fill this house with sorrow--if you dare to sin against your father and your mother----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: One moment, Pastor. My father and my mother--what do you know about them? My father I don't know myself, but my mother? Ah yes, I know her well; and from her I have inherited my life's melody. This melody has a beautiful text. Do you want to know what it is, Pastor? It is, "Thou shalt steal. Steal everything for thyself--thy life's happiness--thy love--all--all. Only others will enjoy it in the end." Yes, Pastor, my mother is a thief. On St. John's eve she came stealthily over yonder garden hedge; and as my mother, so am I! And now, Pastor, ask me no more; I need all my senses, for to-day my entire happiness is at stake! There--now you know all!

div.head: Pastor.
div.p: Yes, now I know! Farewell, Miss Marie. I will forget this day, perhaps; you--never----
[Exit.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Enters door L.] Was that George, who just now left?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Were you at that door, listening?

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: Marie!--For shame!!!!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Now go and dress yourself; I will call George. Go now, go!

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: And will you come and tell me at once?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: At once! Yes!! [Gertrude exits.] [Marie calling softly.] George! George!

div.head: George.
div.p: [Enters from veranda.] Are you alone?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Nods.]

div.head: George.
div.p: Have you arranged it so?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: You wished to speak to me, so I have arranged it!

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie, I wished to tell you. One hour more I am a free man--and my mind is made up. It is yet time to change our fates. What will you answer me?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Answer you? Why, I don't know what you want.

div.head: George.
div.p: You know it well enough. I want you! Do you hear me? You, who belong to me for life--I want you!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Softly--happily.] I thought the fires were out--and you had forgotten me--and now you want me?

div.head: George.
div.p: [Softly.] Are you not mine? Are you not my wife in the eyes of heaven?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, but in the eyes of the world it is Gertrude!

div.head: George.
div.p: Must it, then, be so?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Doubtingly.] Go--go--you love her----

div.head: George.
div.p: Yes, I do love her. How could I help that? Do you not also love her?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Bitterly.] Ah, I don't know. A few moments ago, when I saw her in your arms--and you wept, too--only, because you love her!! Oh, but I can bear it!! I will bear it like--like--ah!---- But there--that is no one's affair but mine----

div.head: George.
div.p: So, so, that is no one's affair but yours, eh? You might have invented a sweeter torture. I meant to remain an honorable man all my life; if unable--well, there are plenty of bullets left.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: And do you wish to die?

div.head: George.
div.p: I do not want to, I must!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: George, then take me with you? [He shakes his head.] For years I have carried the wish in my heart--to kill you! Then I would kiss and love you like mad--and then follow you into eternity----

div.head: George.
div.p: Nonsense, girl, nonsense! Can't you see, how one turns round and round and round in a circle, till at last to find no other escape than death?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: I am not afraid to die; though with you, I'd rather live----

div.head: George.
div.p: To live, dear, will require more courage for both of us.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: How so?

div.head: George.
div.p: Can you ask? Here in this house, to which we owe everything--both you and I? Where they gave us food, shelter and love? After all that, would you have the courage to destroy their happiness?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: The good old pastor used to say: "You must have the courage to do everything, except to do wrong." I would even have the courage to do wrong.

div.head: George.
div.p: Shall I put you to the test?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: If you will give me your hand now and say to me: "Come, we will run away, through yonder garden gate--just as we are--now, this very moment"--you shall see how I will run!

div.head: George.
div.p: What?--Secretly--without telling any one? Is that what you mean?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Don't you?

div.head: George.
div.p: [Laughs bitterly.] No, no!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Well, what then?

div.head: George.
div.p: Face to face, like a man. There he stands--I here. If he will give me back my word, 'tis well. If he refuses [determined], 'tis also well.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: My God! You know his temper! He will kill us--he will kill us both!

div.head: George.
div.p: 'Tis death either way----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: George--think----

div.head: George.
div.p: Oh, I have thought of it for two days and two nights. One is madness and the other insanity. There is no other way. [Pained.] Only the thought of the child gives me pain----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Of course, if your feelings for Gertrude----

div.head: George.
div.p: Then it is your desire? [She nods assent.] Very well! So be it! But remember, it is a question of life and death!--And, therefore, you yourself must be present.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [In terror.] I?--I be present when you ask him?

div.head: George.
div.p: What?--You, who wish to become my helpmate and partner in life, and share all my life's troubles--you would desert me now--desert me in this hour?--and I very much fear, not the worst in store for us?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: No, no, George; it's not that--not that! But you know how we have feared him and have trembled for years--and now I should----

div.head: George.
div.p: If you can't even do that----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: If necessary--yes I--I will do it.

div.head: George.
div.p: Then--as soon as he returns. [ Brauer is heard breathing heavily.] Ah, here he is!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Enters.] Why, that is almost an old-time Biblical miracle. Just think, children, think of it---- But where is Gertrude? Well? Can't you speak?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Trembling.] I think she is dressing!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Well, it will interest you also, so listen: I met the assistant pastor as he came from the house here, and he told me, rather piqued, that our good old pastor had suddenly risen from his bed and limpingly insisted upon delivering the wedding discourse himself. Well--what's the matter? Aren't you glad?

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Of course, you are a perfect heathen! But I say, our assistant pastor must have been terribly put out. He had been preparing for that same address for days. He looked rather crestfallen; but then, there is no help for it.

div.head: George.
div.p: Pardon me, uncle; in order to save time, I must ask you for an interview.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: What, again? Can't you wait till afternoon?

div.head: George.
div.p: No! Before the ceremony, if you please.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Startled.] Wha--oh, I see. I suppose now you will demand more than I am willing to give? Marie, leave us [Paul enters.] Well, what now?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: [Gives him a sign.]

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: There, look at him! Well, have you lost your tongue, man? Why don't you speak?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: No, no, Mr. Brauer, I have something to say to you--alone.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Then why don't you come nearer?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: [Whispering.] We have just now caught the old woman.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [With a glance at Marie.] What? Marie, you may remain and chat with George for awhile; he is a very interesting young man. [Softly, to Paul.] Where?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: Down in the cellar; just as I wanted to put the beer on the ice, I found her there in a dark corner, loaded down with plunder!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Is she there now?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: Yes, struggling like a demon.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Undoubtedly this offense will earn her a good long term in prison and we will be rid of her for a long time! But how to get her out of the house?

div.head: Paul.
div.p: Leave that to me Mr. Brauer; I know a way to keep her quiet.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Yes, yes, and in the meantime I will make out the papers and we will hand her over to the Gendarme; that will be the best. Children, I will be busy for a moment! Wait here until I return.

div.head: George.
div.p: Don't forget, uncle!

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: No, no. I'll be back in a moment. Come, Mr. Paul!
[Both exit.]

div.head: George.
div.p: You are trembling----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Am I?

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie dear, I am with you. No one shall harm you!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Oh, it is not that.

div.head: George.
div.p: What, then?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Oh, I don't know. It has suddenly come over me so---- [Starts.] Sh! He's coming! [Noise. Scuffling of feet and smothered cries are heard.]

div.head: George.
div.p: What is it?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: In God's name, be still!

div.head: Gypsy.
div.p: [Calling for help.] Mine daughter! Mine Mamie! My Mamie!!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Hear? Hear? My mother! They are taking her away--to prison! Sh! Be still! No, no; don't open the door! Be quiet! Be quiet!

div.head: Gypsy.
div.p: [Not as loud as before.] Oh, mine daughter! My Mamie--my Mamie----! [Dying out.]

div.head: George.
div.p: Will you not go out to her, no matter what she has done?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: How can I? How can I? I am afraid--afraid----

div.head: George.
div.p: Then shall I go?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Frightened.] No, no; don't leave me!! Sh! Be quiet! So, quiet! Now they have gone! Thank heaven! [Again wailing, but very distant.] Hear? Hear? Let her shriek! Let her call! I cannot help her! I am a thief, the same as she. I, too, have come to this house, and I have stolen. But oh, my God, what have I stolen? What have I stolen?

div.head: George.
div.p: Come, Marie, control yourself! Think of what we have before us!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, yes--I'll be quiet! What have we before us? No, no; I will not--I cannot--I----

div.head: George.
div.p: Do you mean to----

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [In door.] Did you hear anything, children? Any noise?

div.head: George.
div.p: We heard screams and a scuffle. What was the matter?

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Oh, nothing of any consequence. Don't mind it. An old vagabond of a woman, that's all. I have only to sign the papers now, then I'll be back. [Exit.]

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Hush, not a word, not a word! She out there must go her way, and I must go mine!

div.head: George.
div.p: What do you mean?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: You said it yourself. 'Tis madness! Yes, yes; 'tis madness! All--all! What we do--what we desire--all--all!

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Or do you imagine for one moment we could be happy together? No, I know you too well. I know the certain result. You would never forgive yourself nor me, and in the end life would become a burden to me, if only because I was in your way. Yes, yes, that would be the end of it all----

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie, I will be faithful to you forever, let come what may, be it good or bad; you know that!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Yes, thank God!--yes!

div.head: George.
div.p: If there was only the slightest possibility of a chance to escape from all this whirl--then we might be free, we might---- But no matter what we begin, we cannot shake off nor disregard our obligations to this house; never, as long as we live!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Therefore, what more can you desire? Everything on earth we possess, all that was beautiful, all the love, all--all, we gave to each other. There is nothing more to give, for either one of us. St. John's night is past, the fires are out, are dead----

div.head: George.
div.p: And what shall become of us?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Of you? That I can't tell. Perhaps you will be happy, perhaps not; that must all rest with yourself. And I? Oh, be content. I will take care of myself. As soon as possible I shall leave this house. Not to-day, as I would like--it might create suspicion----

div.head: George.
div.p: And where will you go?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Ah, the world is large. I shall go far, far away, where no one will ever find me. No, no, not even you, George.

div.head: George.
div.p: And if you should go to ruin out there?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: Do not fear. I am the calamity child, the foundling. My hands are hard and callous--see, see! Just like my heart is, now. I will work and work, and toil, until I fall exhausted--then I will sleep and rest, until it is time for work again; and thus I will perhaps maintain a miserable existence.

div.head: George.
div.p: You say you are a calamity child! Well, so am I. But our accounts do not harmonize. You are going out into the world and misery, and it was I who drove you to it. Even did I not love you as I do, that thought would follow me forever and embitter my entire life. But, be it so. We are both children of misery! Therefore let us grit our teeth, shake each other by the hand--and say farewell!

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Softly.] Good-bye, Georgie dear--and--don't be afraid--he is not yet coming--and forgive me--do you hear? From to-day--you understand? Did I not love you as much as I do, this would not have been quite so hard; but there--there--'tis all right now--I know; I can never be entirely poor now; for once, at least, the fires of St. John have burned for me--once--just once----

div.head: George.
div.p: Marie----

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Glancing around.] Don't--don't----

div.head: Mrs. Brauer.
div.p: [Enters, followed by Gertrude.] Hasn't the carriage arrived yet, children? And where is papa? It is time to go.

div.head: Marie.
div.p: He is coming now, I believe.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: [Enters.] So there, I am ready to go! But, that is, you wanted to speak to me first?

div.head: George.
div.p: [With a glance at Marie.] It is all settled now, thank you.

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Then come, wife, my coat, quick!
[She helps him with frocks after he has divested himself of jacket.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Aside to Marie.] Did you ask him?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: [Nods.]

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: And what did he say?

div.head: Marie.
div.p: It was all nonsense, my pet. He loves you and only you. He never has loved any one else--he says--and he will be very happy--so he says----

div.head: Gertrude.
div.p: [Embraces him joyfully.] My darling George----

div.head: Brauer.
div.p: Come, come, my child--time enough for that after the ceremony. Come!

[All follow him to the door. When George reaches door he turns, and as he takes one parting glance at Marie, Brauer pushes him off. Marie stands motionless, looking after them, handkerchief in mouth, nervously forcing it between her teeth.]
[Curtain.]
